title: Why an Ant Survives a Skyscraper Fall | Why It Happens #9
simplified: Simplified model: speeds on the meter are rounded; the ant's top speed is an estimate (university physics estimate plus a drag-equation check).

hook_candidates.text: This ant fell off a skyscraper. So why is it walking?
An ant can't fall fast enough to get hurt.
You'd never survive this fall. This ant shrugs it off.
Drop an ant and a person from the same roof.
Watch this meter. The ant never gets past jogging speed.

parts.text: This ant fell off a skyscraper.
You'd reach two hundred kilometres an hour.
The ant tops out almost at once,
and an ant is nearly all surface.
Scale the ant up to your size.
Its weight grows far faster than its surface.
Now the fall would break it.
parts.tts: Now, the fall would break it.

sources: Ant survives a skyscraper fall: asked about an ant dropped off the Empire State Building, 'The terminal velocity for an ant in air is quite small -- no more than two meters per second' and 'the ant will have no trouble surviving that fall'. University of Illinois Physics Van, 'An ant Dropped off the Empire State Building', https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/2099

'Slower than you jog': 2 m/s = 7.2 km/h (typical jogging is faster). Drag-equation check v = sqrt(2mg / (rho Cd A)) with an ant of about 5 mg, A about 2e-5 m^2, Cd about 1, rho 1.2 kg/m^3 gives about 2 m/s. Labelled estimate.

Person: 'In a spread-eagle position, that terminal velocity may decrease to about 200 km/h' (about 350 km/h head-first). OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1, 6.4 Drag Force and Terminal Speed, https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/6-4-drag-force-and-terminal-speed

Gravity scales with volume, air drag with surface: 'the force of gravity scales with volume (since this is proportional to the total mass)', 'while the force of air resistance scales with surface area'; doubling size: gravity goes up as length cubed, drag as length squared. University of Illinois Physics Van (above). Haldane, 'On Being the Right Size' (1926), quoted in OpenStax 6.4: 'the resistance presented to movement by the air is proportional to the surface of the moving object'; 'A rat is killed, a man is broken, and a horse splashes.'
Shown, not spoken: ten times longer means a hundred times the surface and a thousand times the weight (square-cube law, same sources).

Shown, not spoken: the 'GIANT ANT' meter climbing to about 95 km/h is illustrative. Terminal speed grows with the square root of size (v ~ sqrt(L)), so an ant scaled about 150 times longer would fall about 12 times faster than 7 km/h, roughly 85-95 km/h.
comment_question: Have you ever seen a small animal or insect fall and just walk away?
